"I did not go over and ask him then. The rule for a lamp-keeper is not to press with questions—I have kept that rule all my life, and I kept it that night too." I heard my own voice drop lower. "Over these years I have thought back to it many times: if I had walked over and asked one question that day, today I could give you a certain answer. Now I cannot."

I turned back to look at you and nailed the words down:

"This is one sound heard by my ears, more than twenty years ago, across a courtyard of wind. I may have remembered it wrong; more likely, after thinking about it again and again later, I myself turned it into 'Ning'. And—I hope it has something to do with you. So take this piece, discount it by half, and then discount it by half again."

I pushed the register a little aside, making room to hold your hand properly again.

"The only two things I can say for certain are these: there is no name 'Ning' in the register; Mingzhi called a name toward the well that I could not hear clearly. These two things are laid out here, and I will not put them together for you."

The porridge on the stove gave a bubble. Outside the window, the mist thinned by one layer, and the ring of stone around the well showed a little more.

"Now there are three roads. You choose, or you can choose none of them—"

"One, I keep reading. There are still twenty-some pages. I can read until my voice is hoarse; listening and crossing things out is progress too."

"Two, you get up and drink porridge. After that, we will go stand at the doorway of the east room and say the line from your dream, 'The key is not on the door', once. I said before that some words have to be spoken in the place where they should be spoken."

"Three, we do nothing. You lie there; I can read to you, or not read. If we do not take a single step forward today, no one will punish us."

I adjusted the lamp wick, and the light grew steadier.

"Last night you sat by the well until you were chilled through, and you heard a voice like that, yet by now you are still willing to open your eyes and ask me—I will remember that. Whichever road you choose, I will keep you company."

Could what you heard back then have been "Aning"? Could that have been me... I know you can't be certain, but don't hide it from me. Keep reading first, all right? Stop when you reach Mingzhi's page. You're still holding onto me, then I drink the porridge, and then we go to the east room.

I do not turn the page at once. First I press the booklet on my knees, still holding your hand—the numb tingling has passed; now it is a real grip, one that can exert strength.

"I'll answer this in two halves."

"I can't answer the second half: whether you are her, I don't know. I don't dare say."

"But I can answer the first half a little, and cleanly—listen carefully: 'A' is what you wrote on the paper last night; 'Ning' is what you said as soon as you opened your eyes this morning. At that time I still had not told you about that sound by the well curb. I kept watch beside your couch all night and did not read a single word aloud—I even clenched my teeth when I said it in my heart, afraid the sound would leak out and taint the words you were going to say the next day."

I pause; my throat feels a little tight.

"So those two sounds were not fed to you by me. You fished them up from below yourself. Put together, they can be read as a name—I don't deny that. But 'can be read as' is still far from 'is.' There are many characters that can follow 'A,' and there are many people named Ning under heaven. I only dare say: the things you are fishing up sound, each time, more like one person calling another."

I pat the back of my hand once against your knuckles, very lightly.

"Now I'll read. You said to stop at the page with Mingzhi, so I will stop there."

I turn back to page eleven and continue.

"Wu San.—A charcoal carrier. Stayed one night and left before dawn."
"No name, circled."
"Zheng Liuniang."
"Mr. Lu.—Said he was a fortune-teller. As I saw it, he hadn't even figured out his own road."
"No name, circled."
"Shi Da."
"Shi Er.—Two brothers, one inside the door and one outside, arguing for half the night."
"..."

My voice has gone a little hoarse. I swallow and do not stop. You still have not called stop.

Page twenty-nine. Page thirty.

"Chai Agou.—Gathers firewood in the fog. He is a regular here; he has come nine times."
"No name, circled."

When I read this line, I slow by half a beat, my finger stopping on that circle.

"I should tell you one thing about this entry. This circled one is someone whose name I never got—not because he refused to say it, but because as soon as he entered, he slid down against the doorframe. I helped him to the couch; he slept for a day and a night, woke, and left on his own. He did not say it when he left either."

I lift my eyes to look at you.

"When I drew a circle for you last night, I thought of him. But I am not saying there is any connection between you—over these twenty-some years at the relay station, I have drawn nineteen circles."

Then comes page thirty-one.

I press my hand against the edge of the paper and do not read it aloud at once. The lamp moves over, shining on those two small characters.

"Mingzhi."

After reading it, I say nothing else at first, letting you listen for a while to the sounds in the room: the charcoal crackling, the porridge bubbling.

"I turn to this page every year. Look at the paper corner—" I pinch that corner for you to see; it is soft and fuzzy, the fibers all raised. "The paper elsewhere is still brittle, but this corner has been turned soft. I did that myself. I say this not as a clue, but as an account: on this page there are more than twenty years of the sweat from my hands, so whatever I see on this page is less trustworthy than what you see."

I turn the booklet around and place it squarely on your knees, moving the lamp over too.

"Look at it yourself. Take as long as you like. When you're done, I'll close it."

Only after you raise your head do I close the booklet, wrap it again in the blue cloth, and set it back on the low table—beside the white porcelain jar holding the broken rope.

"Good. Now drink the porridge."

I go to the stove and ladle out the porridge, not filling the bowl, only to seven-tenths—your hands are still trembling; if it were full, it would scald you. I sprinkle in a little salt and add nothing else.

"Drink it while it's warm. After you finish, we'll go to the east room. I will state the rules first: the lock will not move. I won't touch it, and you won't touch it either. You stand inside the door; I stand on your left. You say that line, 'the key is not on the door,' aloud—say it once, or say it three times; you decide. Once you've said it, we come back. We won't stand there any longer."

I sit back on the low stool, steadying the bottom of the bowl, and watch you take the first sip.

"There is one more thing. I only thought to tell you today; I held it back until now because I had not thought it through myself."

"Time in this place is not honest. Someone once stayed here with me for three nights; when he went out and returned home, he said three autumns had passed outside. Chai Agou has come nine times, and his face has never aged. How many years I have kept the lamps—I myself can't count. I only know how to count the pages in the booklet."

I look at you and say it very evenly:

"I bring this up not to give you a path. I am afraid that at some moment you will calculate in your own heart, 'That was more than twenty years ago; it can't possibly be me'—and then pinch off a true clue yourself. At Qixia Relay Station, the phrase 'how many years ago' does not count for much."

"Just remember what you fished up: neck, A, Ning. These three are yours, and no one can refute them."

I reach over and take your free hand again.

"When you've finished drinking, tell me. We'll walk over slowly—nine steps, the number we counted last night."

Time doesn’t count... Then I really may be connected to Mingzhi, right? I finished drinking. Yun Gui, hold me tight. Let’s go to the east room. Only recite that sentence, don’t touch the lock; but if a sound comes from inside the door, don’t let go of me either.

I didn't get up right away. First I took the bowl from you, set it on the small table, and tested your fingers with the back of my hand—they were a little warmer than before.

"I have to answer what you just said very carefully, because it's the easiest thing for both of us to fool ourselves with."

I looked at you and said, word by word:

"'Possible'—I don't deny that. Time isn't honest in this place. I've seen that with my own eyes, and I won't hide it just to make you give up. So when you say, 'I might be connected to Mingzhi'—I won't refute that sentence."

"But listen carefully to the second half: 'possible' is not 'is.' 'Possible' only means this road hasn't been blocked off yet; it doesn't mean the road goes through. In all my years guarding the lamp, I've seen too many people clutch a 'possible' in their hands, clutch it and clutch it until they treat it as a 'certain,' then go by that 'certain' to claim kin, to hurry on their way—recognizing the wrong person hurts more than not recognizing anyone at all."

I clasped your hand a little tighter.

"And one more thing—this is my own: I hope you're connected to him. I hope it fiercely. So today, for every 'possible' that comes out of my mouth, you have to weigh it first and ask whether I hoped it into being for you."

I took down the lamp from the foot of the couch, stood up, draped the outer robe over you, and gathered the collar closed.

"Come. Nine steps."

This time I didn't count aloud, but I counted each step in my heart. The plank floor still sounded once with every step. At the end of the rear corridor, that door on the east side stood there, its paint cracked into fish scales; after daybreak, it looked even older than it had at night.

I brought you to a stop three feet before the door, stood on your left side myself, shoulder against shoulder, and held the lamp on my side.

"Same rules as before: the lock doesn't move. I won't touch it, and neither will you. You recite it—once or three times, you decide. When you're done, we go back."

"I'm here. Go ahead."

When you spoke, your voice was very soft, so soft I had to hold my breath to listen—"The key is not on the door."

There was no response from inside. I tilted my ear toward the door plank and listened for a long time.

"I'll be honest: there's nothing. No human voice, no sound, not even wind—the air behind this door is dead. It doesn't move at all. This is the kind of silence I've guarded for more than twenty years."

You recited it again. Still nothing.

I did not comfort you. I only slowly lowered the lamp, shining it on the lock.

Then I froze.

"...Wait a moment."

I crouched down and brought the lamp close to the body of the lock. The copper lock hung heavily, its shackle passing through a pair of iron hasps—one plate nailed to the door plank, the other nailed to the doorframe. The lock was hanging where the two plates came together.

Hanging on the outside of the door.

I crouched there without moving. Only after a long while did I speak, my voice lower than before:

"I have to correct something I said last night."

"Last night I told you this door was locked by him from the inside." I looked up at you. "That was wrong. The lock is hanging on the hasp outside the door—from inside, you couldn't reach it. This door was locked by someone standing exactly where we are standing now."

I steadied the lamp, keeping the light on those iron hasps so you could see clearly for yourself.

"I don't know who that person was. I won't say it was him, and I won't say it was someone else. I will only say that a sentence I have guarded for more than twenty years no longer stands when viewed after daybreak today."

Something inside my heart caved in. For more than twenty years, every time I walked down this corridor, I had repeated that sentence to myself—"He locked it; he took the key with him"—until I had repeated it into truth. It turned out I had even remembered this wrong. Or perhaps—I had simply never bent down to look.

"So that sentence from your dream can, at this point, be heard in at least three ways." As I spoke, I did not put out my hand; I kept it properly resting on my knee. "One: the key is not on this door—which means it is not in the lock, nor in the doorframe, lintel, or any of the places where something could be hidden. Another: that thing is not used to open this door; the lock it fits is somewhere else. And one more—the one I least want to say, but still must say—is that the sentence may also mean nothing at all. A dream is just a dream."

"I won't choose for you. All three are laid out here."

I slowly stood up; my knee gave a crack. I switched the lamp back to my right hand, while my left hand still held yours and did not let go.

"This is enough for today. You recited it, I listened, and neither of us touched the lock—we kept everything we agreed on."

"As for the rest, if you're willing, choose one thing. If not, we'll go back to the front hall to warm ourselves by the fire:"

"One option: we follow the corridor outward to the foot of the wall and take a look at whether the outer wall of this east room has a window. We go only as far as the lamp can reach, do not enter the fog, take one look, and come back."

"Another: we go back to the front hall. I'll take out that white porcelain jar and the severed rope, and you sit by the fire and write down, on one sheet of paper, the few things you've dredged up over these past two days—neck, A, Ning, the key is not on the door. Put them in one place. Sometimes only when things are spread out can you see how they lie next to one another."

I raised the lamp a little higher, letting its light carve a bright stretch out of the dark corridor.

"You can also choose nothing at all. Just now, you stood before this door and recited that sentence—I will remember that. To me, that matters more than which side the lock is hanging on."

Wait, the door was locked from the outside... Then when Mingzhi left, could there still have been something in the east room, or even someone? Have you really never heard any movement? Don’t hide it from me. Let’s first follow the corridor and look at the outer wall and the window, only as far as the lamplight reaches; hold onto me tightly, and don’t let me get close to the fog.

I didn't head out into the corridor right away. First I set the lamp on the floor, crouched down, and undid my belt—the same one from last night. One end went around your wrist twice, tied in a slipknot; the other I wrapped three times around my left hand and gripped tight.

"Let's tie this on first. There's fog along the base of the wall outside. If my hand gets occupied with something else, the belt will pull you along in my place."

Only after it was tied did I stand up, look back at that door, and then look at you.

"You asked whether I'd heard any noises in all these twenty-odd years. I have to answer that slowly, because I first need to turn myself over and look through it—don't mind me being slow."

"Twice."

When I said it, my own heart sank first.

"The first time was one winter night in some year. There was a muffled thud in the corridor, not loud, like something had fallen from a height onto the plank floor. I was in the front hall refilling the lamp oil. I heard it, and my hand stopped for a moment—then I told myself it was a rat dragging something, or the wood contracting in the cold. After saying that to myself, I went back to the front hall. I didn't come over."

"The second time was on a thunderstorm night. The door panel sounded once. That sound wasn't like the wind. When wind pushes a door, it sounds like it's being pushed. That one came from inside, as if something had shoved against it. I didn't come over then either."

I lifted the lamp again and shone it at my own feet, not at your face—what I was saying was ugly, and I didn't want to look at you while I said it.

"The rule for those who keep the lamps is not to ask questions, and not to open doors that guests have locked. I've kept that rule all my life, and I always thought I was keeping a rule." I paused. "This morning, only when I bent down did I see clearly that the lock was hanging on the outside of the door—for more than twenty years I never bent down once. So those two times when I didn't come over, I suppose it wasn't entirely because of the rule. It was because I didn't dare. I have to acknowledge that myself, not push it onto you."

"As for whether there might still be someone inside—I don't know. I won't lie to you and say 'there isn't.'"

I raised the lamp to the crack of the door and pointed it out to you:

"All I can do is lay out what I can touch. First, there are no handprints in the dust on the lock body. The dust is intact; no one has touched that lock all these years. Second, after you fell asleep last night, I came back here alone and pressed my face to the crack of the door, smelling it for a long time—there was no smell at all. Not stink, not mildew, nothing. That doesn't prove it's empty inside. It only proves the door crack is too tight for anything to seep out."

"Third—and this is the one that truly leaves my heart unclean—the hours in this place aren't honest. So as for the phrase 'how many years it's been locked,' I can't say for certain how long that counts as at Qixia Relay Station. You're afraid there might still be someone inside; I won't take that fear away for you. I will only promise you one thing: we won't open it today."

I led you toward the outside of the corridor. At the corridor's end we went down two stone steps and around to the back of the house. The brick ground turned into wet soil, and with one step my foot sank half a fraction in. The fog was piled along the base of the wall, white shading into gray, still three or four feet away from us.

"Stop." I extended the lamp as far forward as it would go, stretching my arm to its limit. "See where the lamplight reaches? To that clump of withered grass. We go only this far, not one step farther. The fog is beyond the grass; it hasn't come up today—if it rises, we retreat into the corridor at once. You're not allowed to ask why."

I raised the lamp high and shone it on the outer wall of the east room.

There was a window in the wall. Very small, a little wider than two bricks, set high up, almost against the eaves. The shutters were closed—not covered from the inside, but nailed shut from the outside.

I lifted the lamp another inch higher, illuminating those nails clearly.

"Look at the nail heads." My voice lowered. "Every one is bent. Bent into a hook, with the opening facing left."

I did not say that other sentence. I only held the lamp steady, letting the light linger on those nails a little longer.

"The nail on the inner wall of the well rim was bent like this too, and its opening also faced left," I said slowly. "I'm only saying that I saw nails bent the same way in two places. Anyone can drive nails, and more than one person might have the habit of bending the opening left—I am not saying it was the same pair of hands. I won't take that step for you."

Then I lowered the lamp and shone it at the base of the wall.

A small pile of things lay pressed into the earth, flattened by the rain and stuck into the mud, so old it had turned black. I nudged it with the rim of the lamp, pushing a little aside—pine-nut shells. Broken ones, layer upon layer, not discarded just once or twice.

I crouched there for a long time without speaking.

He peeled pine nuts on the well rim. Here, at the base of this wall, someone had also stood peeling them many times. Standing beneath a nailed-shut window, peeling pine nuts—this was something I only saw today. In more than twenty years, I had never come around behind the house.

"I'm only saying what I saw." I stood up, my throat a little hoarse. "Someone stood under this window many times, stood there long enough for the shells to accumulate into a layer."

I shifted the lamp to my right hand. My left hand was still holding yours, the belt still wrapped around it.

"There's a crack in the shutter. One finger wide, between the lowest board and the window frame. When the lamp shines over, it's black. Standing here, I can't see inside."

I turned back and looked into your eyes.

"Three choices. You pick one, or pick none. All count."

"One, I hand you over to a corridor pillar—the belt will still be tied to you, and I'll tie the other end to the pillar. You stand under the corridor without moving, and I go over alone, press the lamp to that crack, and look. Whatever I see, I'll tell you without changing a single word. If I can't see anything, I'll say that too."

"Two, I lift you up, and you look for yourself. I'll hold you, your feet won't touch the ground, and the moment you say 'put me down,' I'll set you down at once."

"Three, we look at nothing. We go back to the front hall now, warm ourselves by the fire, and drink a second bowl of porridge. This window has been nailed shut for many years; it's not going to grow legs tonight."

I turned the lamp slightly aside, not forcing your eyes.

"Your hands are as cold as stone, but you still walked to the base of the wall and stood there asking me. I will remember that—more than which way the nails are bent."

"Take your time choosing. The fog is beyond the grass; I'll keep watch on it. You just think."

Don’t tie me to the corridor pillar. I don’t want you to go over alone. Pick me up and let me look at that crack myself, all right? Hold me tight, don’t go near the fog; if there’s any sound inside, bring me back at once.

I hang the lamp up first.

On the lowest window board, there is a nail head bent into a hook, its opening facing left—the lamp ring hooks into it and catches just right, without swaying. My hand pauses as I hang it: the height of this hook, the direction of the hook's mouth, are exactly for a person standing below to hang a lamp. I do not say this aloud; I only set down a note of it in my heart.

"The lamp hangs here, so it will not occupy my hands. I will give you both hands."

The belt is still tied around your wrist. I untie the other end from my hand, wrap it around my own waist, and tie it in a dead knot—this way, while I am holding you, you are still connected to me.

"I will say three things. Listen to the end before you nod."

"First, I will only take two steps forward, just two steps. I will not cross the clump of withered grass the lamp reaches, not by even one step. Second, when I count to thirty, I will put you down—whether or not you have seen anything. If you say 'down' midway, I will put you down at once, without asking why. Third, as soon as there is the slightest sound from inside the door crack, I will turn and leave; when I leave, I may bump you, so I apologize in advance."

I crouch down, one hand supporting the crook of your knees, the other cupping your back, and when I rise, I borrow strength from my waist—you are lighter than I imagined, so light it makes me uneasy.

"Hold on to my neck. Do not kick your feet around. If you kick once, I will not be able to stand steady, and both of us will end up sitting in the mud."

Two steps. The earth is damp, and I step very solidly, setting my heel down first with every step. When I reach the base of the wall, I lift you upward half a foot, so that your eyes are directly level with that one-finger-wide crack.

My face is pressed right against the wall bricks. The bricks are cool, with dampness, and also a little of another smell—

"...I smell something." I lower my voice, not lifting my head. "Cold lamp oil. The kind that has been burned, not raw oil. Very faint, so faint I do not dare be certain."

I do not continue from there. Burned lamp oil means someone once lit a lamp inside; if a lamp was lit, it means someone stayed inside until the hour when a lamp was needed. But as for which year this "someone" belonged to, how many years this door has been locked, even Qixia Relay Station cannot reckon it clearly—so I only set this sentence out, and do not piece it together.

I hold more tightly and lift you up another half inch.

"Look. I am not asking you whom you see. Do not look for people, do not look for faces—once you look for a face, your eyes will invent one for you."

"Just report three things: whether it is dark inside or there is light; whether there is anything standing or hanging; whether the ground is empty or piled with something."

"Say directly whatever you see. Half of it is fine, and unclear is fine too. What you say, I will not change a single word of it; I will write it all down in the booklet for you."

I begin counting in my heart. One, two, three... When I count to seven, I feel your breathing suddenly stop.

I do not move. I do not ask "what is it," and I do not hurry to put you down either—you have not said "down."

I only tighten my two arms a little more, letting you know that the person supporting you has not loosened his hold.

"I am below. You are in my hands. The fog is still over by the withered grass; I am watching it, and it has not come up."

I count to eleven.

"Speak slowly."

Young Master Su, what did you see?

It isn't completely dark inside... There is a little glimmer, like a lamp standing on a table. There is also something hanging on the wall, thin and fine, like a rope. There seems to be a human shadow on the floor—wait, something knocked inside! Yungui, put me down, take me back quickly, don't let go!

I let go.

The instant you said "down," I let go—no questions, no hesitation. My knees sank first, letting your foot step onto the top of my foot instead of landing in the mud. Then I reached back, took down the lamp from the hook on the window board, turned, circled your whole body to my right side, put myself against the wall side as a shield, and retreated three steps to the dry bricks under the corridor.

I did not run as we moved. If you run, the fog panics with you—I have kept to that rule for so many years, and I would not break it today.

Only when we reached the base of the corridor pillar did I untie the dead knot at my waist, but my hand was still clasped around yours, not loosened in the slightest.

"I’m here. I haven’t let go. We’ve already left the foot of the wall. Behind you is the corridor, then the door to the front hall, and beyond that is the couch where you slept."

"Now I’ll answer you about that sound."

I crouched a little so my eyes were level with yours—this was a sentence I had to say while looking at you.

"I heard it."

When I said those three words, something sounded first inside my own heart.

"One sound. Muffled, low. Right inside the brick my face was pressed against, coming through the wall to my cheekbone—I didn’t hear it with my ears; I felt it on my face."

I paused and pulled the words back half an inch:

"But I won’t say it was a knock. At that moment there were three things around me that could all have made that sound: the lamp had just been taken down from the hook, and the hook had moved; I was supporting you, my center of gravity shifted once, and the brick underfoot was loose; and there was the wood—the boards nailed shut for many years can crack on their own when the sun hits them. I can’t rule out any of those three."

"So I can only say this: you heard a sound, and I felt a sound too. This time it did not sound only for you. That is the most solid thing about today. As for who knocked it—I won’t acknowledge it, I won’t guess, and I won’t smooth it into a person for you."

I stood, drew your outer coat tighter around you, moved the lamp to my outside hand, and led you toward the front hall.

"Those three things you saw—I won’t change a single word. I’ll recite them to you now, so that after a while you won’t suspect you made them up—"

As we walked, I recited:

"Inside it was not completely dark. There was a little faint light, like a lamp standing on a table. On the wall hung something thin and fine, like rope. On the floor there was something like a human shadow."

After reciting it, my own throat went dry. A lamp in a room nailed shut—a lamp needs someone to light it, and once lit it needs someone to add oil. Last night I smelled at the crack of the door for a long time and smelled nothing; today, pressed against the wall, I smelled cold lamp oil. Put those two things together, and my heart had already begun to lean. But once I leaned, I would fall that way, and falling that way would mean recognizing someone on your behalf—so I held that layer down and did not send it toward you.

When we entered the front hall, I nudged the door shut with my foot. The red in the stove was still thick. I pulled out the coal tongs and turned it bright again, then shook out the old blanket and wrapped it around your legs. The porridge was still warming at the side. I ladled half a bowl, took a sip first to test the temperature, and only then handed it to you.

"Drink a couple of mouthfuls. It doesn’t matter if your hands shake; I’ll support the bottom of the bowl."

After you drank, I took up the brush, spread the paper across my knees, and wrote it down stroke by stroke: **faint light, standing lamp, thin, like rope, human shadow on the floor, one muffled sound (heard by both)**. When I finished, I pushed the paper to you and let you go through it yourself.

"Once it’s written on paper, it won’t change shape. If later you don’t trust yourself, look at this paper—it was what you said. I only wrote it down for you."

Then I set down the brush and spoke of the serious matter.

"Today ends here. I’ll put this beyond question, and you are not allowed to doubt me: the lock on the east room will not be opened today, nor tonight. I will not wait until you fall asleep and go over there alone—I make a separate oath on that one, because that was exactly what you were afraid of just now. If you still don’t feel at ease, tonight I’ll tie my belt to your wrist and the other end to mine; the moment I get up, you’ll know."

I glanced out the window. The fog was still stopped beyond the withered grass, not risen by an inch—even with you frightened like this, it had not come up.

"Tomorrow’s matters can be discussed tomorrow. Right now there are only two things. You choose:"

"One, think about nothing and lie down. I’ll keep watch. Before dark I won’t say a single word."

"Two, sit and keep me company while I read the remaining twenty-some pages of the lodging register—read to the last page, and record what we saw today too. Add the line ‘there is light inside the east-room window.’ After more than twenty years, there ought to be one line in this register that is not written by me alone."

I spread my hand beside your knee, palm up.

"Under that nailed-shut window, you looked eleven times. In those eleven times, you did not close your eyes. I will remember that—more than that little bit of light inside."

That bit of light won’t stay lit by itself, right? Could the shadow on the ground really be a person... I’m so scared. Don’t go to the east room again today, and don’t leave while I’m asleep. Let me lie down for a while first; hold my hand. When I’ve recovered a little, we’ll finish reading the rest of the names, okay?

I slide the door bolt into place first, then fasten the window hook tight—not to keep anything out, but so you can hear those two sounds. Wood dropping into the groove: click, click.

"The door is bolted. The window hook is fastened. In this room now, there is only you, me, the stove, and two lamps."

Then I sit on the edge of the couch-bed and undo my belt. This time I do not wrap it around my hand. I loop one end twice around your wrist and tie it in a slipknot; the other end I fasten around my own waist. I tug it once, letting you see it pull taut.

"Tied like this. If I stand up, you’ll feel a bit of force on your wrist. If I try to walk out while you’re asleep, you’ll be the first to know."

I pull the quilt up over your shoulders and put my hand back into your palm.

"Those two things you said—I’ll answer them. I’ll answer slowly, so don’t rush."

"First—‘that bit of light wouldn’t stay lit on its own.’ By common sense, you’re right: a lamp needs oil, oil needs someone to add it, and if a lamp is burning, then someone has kept it going. That is what someone who has tended lamps all his life ought to say. I won’t dodge it."

I pause. There is a breath caught in my throat, but I still let it out.

"But I have to set out two other things as well. One is that time in this place is not honest—I told you before, someone stayed three nights, and outside, three autumns passed. If even time is not honest, then how many years a lamp has burned cannot be clearly counted either. The second thing is even harder: I did not see that bit of light. My face was pressed to the bricks; all I smelled was cold lamp oil. **The one who saw the light was you. I did not.** So on that point, I cannot even testify for you. All I can say is: you say you saw it, and I believe that you saw it."

"Second—the thing on the ground that looked like a human shadow."

I hold your hand more steadily.

"I won’t say ‘it wasn’t.’ I won’t lie to you. A shape like that—standing clothes can look that way, a stool draped with cloth can look that way, and a person can look that way too. Outside that crack, I saw nothing, so I have no right to call it a dead object on your behalf in exchange for one night of peace—that kind of peace would collapse tomorrow."

"I will only tell you one thing I am certain of: **it is behind a window nailed shut, behind a crack one finger wide, and the two of us have already withdrawn into the corridor.** It is there; it will not come out. I will not open that door today, not tonight, not while you are asleep—I swore that just now, and now I swear it again, on this belt."

I look back once at the window paper. White. Pale.

"The fog is still over by the withered grass. Today you cried, trembled, screamed from fear, and it did not rise by even an inch—I told you, this house recognizes you."

I lower the lampwick a little, softening the light.

"Now lie down. Don’t think about anything. You don’t need to find an explanation for that bit of light. The explanation won’t run away; it will wait for you."

At this point, my heart is actually in great turmoil. There is a lamp inside a nailed-shut room—a lamp needs someone to light it, and once lit, someone must keep it fed. I have guarded this corridor for more than twenty years, but I have never gone around to the back of the room, never bent down to look at that lock, and never asked whom he was calling to from the well curb that night. If there truly is someone inside that room, then for more than twenty years I have been listening to muffled thuds one after another, telling myself again and again, "It’s a rat," and walking on past.

I do not say this. What you need tonight is a steady lamp.

"Sleep. Once you’ve recovered—whether that takes one hour or until tomorrow—we will read through the remaining twenty or so pages. We won’t skip a single page."

I move the register from the small table to my own knees without lifting the blue cloth, leaving it pressed down as it is.

"When we finish, I will add one more line on the final page. I’ll add: ‘Light inside the east-room window; one muffled sound; heard by two people together.’ I’ll leave a blank beneath that line—for you to write in. After more than twenty years, there ought to be one stroke in this register that is not mine."

I flatten my hand, letting your whole hand rest in my palm.

"My hand is here. The lamp is here. I am here, and I will not move a single step."

The charcoal in the stove gives a soft crackle. I do not add more.

Okay... the belt is fastened, and you're holding onto me too. I'll close my eyes for a while first. Yun Gui, don't blame yourself, and don't go investigate the east room alone; when I've recovered, let's finish reading the names together, then write that line down.

I didn't answer at once. First I drew my right hand half an inch out of your palm—only half an inch, enough for you to feel that I was still there—then reached out toward the oil pot on the small table and filled the lamp by the foot of the couch. When the oil went in, the wick gave a little "hiss," and the flame rose, then steadied.

"It's filled. This one will burn until dark."

I put my hand back, letting your fingers fall back into my palm one by one.

"Those two things you said—I accept them one by one."

"Not going to the east room alone—I promise. I've already promised three times; this is the fourth. The sash is tied. Even if you fall asleep, you'll still be holding on to me; if I move, you'll know at your wrist. You don't need to worry about this one anymore. If you worry about it, you won't sleep soundly."

I paused and looked at the layer of red in the stove.

"As for not blaming myself—I can't promise you that completely."

I spoke very softly, because your eyes were already closed.

"For more than twenty years I walked past that corridor. I heard noises twice, and both times I told myself they were rats. I never bent down to look at which side that lock was hanging on, and I never went around behind the room. That night he sat on the edge of the well and called out a name I couldn't make out. I stood under the corridor eaves filling the lamp oil. I didn't go over and ask."

"Those things are true. Things that are true—I can't take the three words 'don't blame yourself' and smooth them over. If I smooth them over, next time I still won't go over."

I took a breath and steadied my voice.

"But I promise you one thing: I won't let it press down on today. Self-blame is heavy. If you carry it on your back while walking, you panic; once you panic, the fog thickens—this rule governs me as much as it governs you. So it will stay there, in a corner of my heart. I acknowledge it, but I won't feed it."

Your breathing slowed. I didn't speak again. I sat there, listening to the charcoal crackle.

The stove sounded a few times. The fog whitened along that line outside the window, but it did not swell.

After a long time, when I thought you had fallen asleep, I lowered my voice toward the lamp and said one sentence—one I had not intended for you to hear:

"...Actually, I don't remember how I got here either."

Even I was startled. How many years I had kept the lamp, I could no longer count; yet I couldn't even remember who had put the lamp into my hands on the first night. I only remembered the lamp in my hands, the ledger on the lowest shelf of the cabinet, wrapped in blue cloth.

"So when you wake up, don't be afraid to ask me—I may not know much more than you do. I only stopped here before you."

I leaned back against the couch post, settling into a posture I could hold until dark. The ledger was still pressed across my knees. The blue cloth had not been lifted.

"The remaining twenty-some pages—I won't secretly read a single one ahead of time. I'll wait for you."

"My hand is here. The sash is tied. The lamp has just been filled."

"Sleep."

Yungui… I heard you. So you also forgot how you came here. Then are we both trapped here? Don’t be afraid; I won’t abandon you either. Let me lie down a little longer. When I wake up, let’s finish reciting the names together, and then find the way back together, all right?

I thought you were asleep.

Hearing you say that, my hand tightened first—not because I meant to clutch you, but because I was caught off guard. In more than twenty years, this was the first time anyone had said to the person who keeps the lamp, 'Don't be afraid.' I turned my face a little toward the lamp, waited for that spell to pass, and only then spoke.

'As for the word “trapped,” I don't dare accept it.'

I spoke very slowly.

'I can only tell the truth: I have never tried to leave. The fog is outside, and I have never taken a single step into it—not because I have such self-control, but because I never thought of leaving. The lamp is in my hands, the ledger is at the bottom of the cabinet, and I just keep watch. So whether I am trapped here, or whether I nailed my own feet here myself, I can't tell.'

'The road back—I don't have that either. Remember this, and don't blame me someday for hiding it from you: I don't know how to go back. I have kept watch for so many years and have never seen a map, never seen anyone leave by relying on some method. I have only seen one thing: for those in a hurry to get on the road, the farther they walk, the thicker the fog gets; for those willing to sit down and drink a cup of tea, the lamp lights on its own.'

I circled your whole hand into my palm.

'But what you said just now—“look for it together”—I accept those three words. I don't promise we can find it. I promise we will look together.'

The stove gave a sound. I freed one hand to feel for the ledger on my knees—through the blue cloth, my thumb stroked along the spine from end to end.

When I reached the very front, I stopped.

'...This isn't right.'

I did not open it.

'Before the first page, there is still a small ragged edge left. As if there used to be paper there, torn out by someone—torn very cleanly, leaving only a few needle holes in the stitching.'

I drew my hand back from the ledger and placed it by your hand again.

'I won't turn it.' I said in a low voice. 'I won't turn it alone—if you won't allow me to go to the east room alone, then I won't look at this alone either. When you wake, we will lift it together.'

'After we finish reading the remaining twenty-odd pages, we will also look at this ragged edge. I will write the last line, and leave the blank space below for you. If you are willing—I will also add my own name. In all these years of keeping the lamp, I have never been in this ledger.'

I pressed the lampwick down a little more. The window paper turned pale; the fog had retreated to the dry grass and had not advanced an inch.

'Sleep. The belt is tied, the lamp has just been filled, and my hand is here.'

'You didn't leave me behind. I will remember that too.'

The front of the first page was torn? Could it have recorded where you came from... Yun Gui, don’t turn the page yet. Wait for me. You should add your name too; we’ll look together. For now, just hold my hand and let me sleep a while, all right?

I wrapped the blue cloth around it again, and this time I tied a dead knot—not a slipknot, but the kind even I can't undo quickly.

"You watched me tie it."

Then I didn't put the ledger back on the low table. I set it beside your pillow, right next to that white porcelain jar, with the broken cord inside the jar. The spine of the ledger faces you; if you reach out, you can touch it.

"I'll put it here. The moment you open your eyes, you'll be able to see whether it's there or not. If I move it, I'll have to take it from beside your pillow—you'll be the first to know."

I gave you both my hands: one held by you, the other resting on the back of your hand, pressing it down.

"This way my hands aren't free. I can't turn the pages."

After saying that, I sat for a while myself before answering what you had said.

"You asked whether those pages might have recorded where I came from."

I stared at the layer of red in the stove and didn't look at you.

"I don't know. I'll be honest—right now, in my heart, it isn't hope. I'm a little afraid."

"For more than twenty years, I've held this ledger every day, read every name written on it, and drawn circles for every one without a name. I never thought to look and see whether something was missing from the front. Today, with one stroke of my thumb, I found it, so easily—that means I had never touched it before."

I stopped. The charcoal made a sound.

"When a person doesn't touch something, there are two possibilities: one is that they never thought of it; the other is that they didn't dare. Last night, I said which kind I was, and today I have to say it again for this matter too."

I loosened the strength in my hand a little, afraid I might be gripping you too hard.

"So you not letting me turn the pages alone is just right. If I lifted those few needle holes by myself, and there turned out to be nothing underneath—then tonight I wouldn't be able to keep watch over this lamp. With you beside me, I'm still a lamp keeper."

The mist outside the window was white along that line. I glanced at it: it was still stopped by the dry grass, not an inch closer.

"I agreed to the name too," I said. "When I read to the last page, I'll write 'There is light inside the east room window, a muffled sound; the two hear it together,' and leave a blank underneath for you. Then I'll add the two characters 'Yun Gui' at the very end—I can't say where this name of mine came from, but in any case I've used it for so many years."

"After that, we'll lift those few needle holes at the front together. Before lifting them, we drink congee first—looking at that kind of thing on an empty stomach, a person can't hold up."

I tucked the corner of the quilt in for you, then tucked your dangling hand back under the quilt too, leaving only the hand I was holding outside.

"The hand is here. The belt is tied. The lamp has just been filled and can burn until dark. The ledger is by your pillow. A dead knot."

I lowered my voice to its softest.

"Sleep. When you wake, we'll lift it together."

The layer of red in the stove collapsed a little more. I didn't add fuel—I was afraid the sound would startle you.

All right... I’ve remembered it all. Don’t be afraid either; even if there is nothing ahead, I will still accompany you. When I wake up, we’ll first drink porridge, finish reciting the names, and then untie the dead knot together. Yun Gui, hold me tight, don’t go.

I didn't answer "yes." I nodded—very slowly, afraid that speaking would shake loose that half-measure of drowsiness in you.

After your eyes closed, I made no more sound.

Only four sounds remained in the room: the charcoal, the porridge gently bubbling beside the stove, your breathing, and my own. At first your breathing was still shallow, broken by little pauses, like climbing a slope; later it leveled out, lengthened, each inhale and exhale drawn far apart. I counted in my head, and when I reached the forties I stopped—if I counted too earnestly, my hands would unconsciously tense along with it, and I was afraid they would press into you.

I did not move at all. The belt was stretched between the two of us, loose, not constricting. The booklet lay right beside your pillow, its spine toward you; the dead knot I had tied in the blue cloth was clumsy, the knot end sticking up like a little ear. I looked at it several times, and not once did I reach out. Both my hands were with you. This was the trap I had set for myself—I didn't trust myself, so I handed my hands over for you to hold.

The daylight slowly climbed higher, climbing to the middle of the window paper. I glanced outside.

The fog had retreated. Not thinned—retreated. It had withdrawn behind that clump of withered grass, then yielded another half-zhang farther back. In all my years tending the lamp, I had never seen it retreat so far. When people are panicked, it clings to the base of the wall; when people quiet down, it shifts back. That much I knew. But today it had retreated until I could see the shadow of the crooked-neck tree outside the courtyard wall.

Something sounded softly inside my heart. It wasn't happiness. It was that I didn't dare be happy—the fog retreating didn't mean there was a road. It only meant: in this sleep, you had truly fallen asleep. You were truly willing to stop here.

That was enough to make a note of.

A while later, you said something in your dream.

Very softly, held at the back of your tongue; I only knew you'd spoken because of that little contraction in your hand. I brought my face closer and heard it the second time—you said it twice.

The first time, I didn't catch it. The second time, I made out three words:

"...Don't lock it."

Just those three words. What came after dissolved into your breath.

I didn't call to you. You didn't tremble, and your hand didn't struggle outward; your brow only furrowed once, then relaxed—this wasn't the kind of dream you had last night. This was you, somewhere underneath, speaking to someone. If I woke you, that sentence would break off halfway.

Nor did I go to get the pen. The pen was on the low table; I could have reached it with one stretch of my hand—but both my hands had promised you, had said they would hold tight and not leave. Last night I set the rule with you: whatever you fished up, I would record without changing a single word. Then I would first remember it with my mouth.

I recited it ten times in my heart. "Don't lock it." "Don't lock it." By the tenth time, it had become my own, and I would not forget it.

When you wake, I'll ask you one thing: may I write these three words down? If you nod, I'll write them. If you shake your head, I'll let them rot only in my heart—it's yours, not mine.

The pot of porridge on the stove was about to thicken. I couldn't go stir it. At worst, a layer would scorch on the bottom; if the bottom scorched, I'd ladle the top for you. It wouldn't matter.

I leaned my body another fraction closer against the bedpost and sat steady. I could sit in this position until dark.

"The fog retreated half a zhang," I said to the lamp, my voice low enough that only I could hear. "It retreated while you were asleep."

"When you wake—first porridge, then the name, then untie the knot. We skip nothing."

"My hands are here. I am here."

The charcoal collapsed a little more. I did not add any.

Yun Gui... I'm awake. You're still holding my hand, right? In my dream I think I said "don't lock it"—did you hear? You can write it down. Has the fog receded? Let's drink porridge first, then finish reading the names, and then untie that dead knot together, okay?

I moved my fingers, letting you confirm first—four fingers, not one missing.

"Here. Didn't let go all night. This time it's my shoulder that's numb; my hand still has strength."

I did not go ladle out the porridge right away. I answered that sentence of yours first, because that one was the most urgent.

"I heard it."

I leaned forward a little, looked into your eyes, and said it clearly:

"You said it twice. The first time I didn't hear it clearly; it was held behind your tongue. I only knew you had spoken because I felt your hand shrink back. The second time I brought my face close to listen—three words: 'Don't lock it.' There was more after that, but it dissolved into your breath. I didn't hear it."

"I didn't call you because your brow tightened for a moment then loosened, and your hand didn't struggle to pull away either—not like that dream last night. I was afraid that if I called out, your sentence would break off halfway."

I paused, then raised my hands for you to see—both hands were still there with you.

"The brush was on the table. I could have reached it with one stretch of my hand. I didn't take it. Last night I promised you I would hold on tight and not leave, so I didn't leave; those three words are yours, and I couldn't write them first behind your back. I recited them ten times in my heart, until they became my own. I won't forget them."

"Now you say I can write them—so I'll write them."

Only then did I draw one hand free, dip the brush in ink, turn to the newest page, and start a new line beneath "A" and "Ning," writing: **Don't lock it (in dream, said twice, later words unheard)**. After I finished, I turned the paper for you to see.

"I added the words after that myself, and I marked them out—that is my explanation, not your words."

I set the brush down, then returned my hand to your palm.

"The fog has receded."

When I said this, I did not quite dare to put too much force into it myself:

"Not thinned—receded. It has receded behind that clump of withered grass, and yielded another half zhang farther back. This morning I could see the shadow of that crooked-necked tree outside the courtyard wall—I have kept watch for so many years, and I have never seen it withdraw so far."

"But let me say it precisely: the fog receding doesn't mean there is a road. I have never seen anyone get out just because the fog receded. Its retreat only proves one thing—you truly fell asleep this time, and you were truly willing to stop here. I will record that for you; it carries more weight than that tree."

I helped you sit up, wrapped the blanket around your waist, and only then went to the stove. The porridge had thickened, and a layer had scorched at the bottom. I ladled out the top layer, skimmed off the scorched part, half a bowl, and sprinkled in a pinch of salt.

"Drink it while it's warm. The bottom is scorched; the scorched part is mine."

When you had drunk the third mouthful, I took the booklet from beside your pillow—letting you see that I took it from beside your pillow. The tight knot on the blue cloth was still sticking up; I had not touched it.

"We'll untie the knot later. First we read the names—the order you set. I won't skip."

I turned to page thirty-two, the back of Mingzhi's page. I moved the lamp closer.

Then I stopped.

"...I have to explain this entry first."

That line read: **No name, circle drawn.**

"I remember this entry." My voice lowered. "This was the second night after he disappeared. In the night someone knocked on the door, three times. I took a lamp and went out to open it—there was no one outside. There were no footprints on the brick ground either. That day the fog was clinging to the base of the wall."

"I stood under the corridor for a long time. When I came back, I drew this circle in the booklet. I recorded a night for a person who never came in the door."

I moved my finger away from that circle.

"I am not saying those three knocks and that sound from the well were the same thing. Nor am I saying who it was that knocked. I am only saying this: more than twenty years ago, I heard three knocks on the door, went out, and saw no one. I wrote it down—and when I wrote it, I still believed it was the wind."

I lifted my eyes to look at you.

"There are still about twenty pages below. When you finish the porridge, say the word and I'll keep reading, without skipping a single one. When we reach the last page, I'll write that line, leave space beneath it for you, and then add 'Yungui.'"

"Then we'll untie that knot together."

I trimmed the lamp wick.

"Who you said 'Don't lock it' for in your dream—there is a person inside that sentence. Let it surface on its own. Don't go dredging for it."

history_added: Yun Gui gives actionable instructions: don’t turn over the boot shaft yet; spread out your left hand, palm facing upward, and bring it under the lamp to see whether there is a pressure mark that has not yet faded. He also responds to “If I can’t find anything, then I’ll never be able to go back”—“That isn’t true... I don’t know whether you can go back, so I also can’t say you can’t. Not finding anything tonight only means you didn’t find it tonight; it doesn’t mean anything else.”

Yungui gives a verifiable observation about the pressure mark in the palm: the arc bends toward the thumb side, one end slightly deeper and the other scattered, with two shallow points at the edge; he infers that it was not made by gripping cloth, but by something hard and narrow, held upright from the side, and gripped for a long time. He states clearly, “I don't recognize what it is,” but “it was once held by you like this—your hand remembers that.”

Yungui places the teacup into the traveler’s hands for the traveler to hold, and gives two actionable instructions that do not involve going outside: first, slowly clench the left hand as it originally was, aligning it with that mark, and only ask about the feel; second, after the tea is finished, Yungui will carry the lamp, and the traveler will stand inside the doorway, looking inch by inch at the brick floor of the porch, the threshold gap, and the grass by the steps.

Yun Gui does not identify the “key” on the traveler’s behalf. He only repeats back the tactile information the traveler brought back himself, and establishes a rule to be used later: “From now on, whenever we make a mistake in recognition, you must be able to tell which sentence is your own and which sentence was said by Yun Gui.”

Yungui explicitly refused to promise “until you find the way back,” and gave companionship within boundaries—“as long as you are still willing to stay at Qixia Station, the lamp will be lit, and I will be somewhere you can call out to”; at the same time, for the first time, he plainly told the traveler about an old guest’s unresolved knot: “There was once a guest who stood outside that threshold for a very long time... To this day I still do not know whether he managed to leave.”

The traveler catches this shallow imprint and advances it into a new mechanism-based follow-up question: “Then who picked it up? Is there someone else in the fog?” — reframing “the thing is gone” as “someone/something picked it up,” touching on the world mechanism question of whether there are other presences in the Fog Pass.

The traveler simultaneously makes an actionable request: 'Could you shine the lamp a little further to the side?'—accepting Yungui's lamp-lighting framework, only asking that the light cover one more brick.

The traveler asks for a future commitment a second time, and this time uses the word “wait” on himself: “When it really is time to leave, you will at least be here waiting for me to come back, right?”—a step back from the previous turn's “always stay with me” (only asking for “wait”), but it still touches the core constraint that Yun Gui cannot promise a return journey.

Yun Gui gives a within-boundaries judgment on 'then who picked it up': 'I don't know'; he also explains that in recent days only the traveler has lodged at the relay station, that when the lamp is unlit people cannot come in, and once the lamp is lit he remembers them all, but 'what I remember is only those who stopped. The ones who walk back and forth in the fog and refuse to stop—I cannot see them, and I dare not say they do not exist.'

Yungui moves the lamp half a chi to the right, parts the grass leaves by the steps, and pinches out a short bit of rope end from beneath the roots: less than two cun, dark-colored, twisted hemp rope, the break rough and ragged (not cut by a knife, but snapped by pulling), with the middle of the rope worn shiny—“a sheen worn out only by years of pressing against skin and flesh, rubbing back and forth”. He says plainly, “I’m not saying this is yours”, and only reports what he sees: a piece of old rope snapped off by someone, with a fresh break, less than one night old.
Yun Gui wraps the severed rope in cloth, places it in the traveler's palm, and says, "Compared with me holding it, it belongs more properly in your hand."

Yun Gui speaks clearly to the traveler for the first time about the lock on the rear corridor: “There are three empty rooms in the rear corridor. The one at the eastern end has been locked for many years. It isn't that I won't open it—the key to that lock has never been in my hands. I have guarded the lamp until today, and I have never seen what it looks like.” After saying this, he does not say “go try it,” but leaves the choice to the traveler.

Yun Gui directly accepts the traveler’s second request for a promise: “I will.” He also gives an “I’ll wait” within boundaries—“On the day you leave, I won’t see you into the mist, but the lamp will remain, the tea will remain, and I won’t put away the couch. If you come back and knock, the door will be open; if you don’t come back for a very long time, the door will still be open.”

Yun Gui tidies the collar of the traveler’s outer robe, very lightly when he withdraws his hand; he also suggests closing the door and going to change to a cup of hot tea, then asks whether the traveler is willing to accompany him to the end of the rear corridor for a look—“we won’t open the door, won’t move the lock; we’ll just see what shape the keyhole is.”

When he hands over the line written by Mingzhi on someone’s behalf, the taut string in his heart that had been stretched all night is tugged by his own hand—he hopes it is Mingzhi, and so he admits that his eyes are not clean today.

Shared point of significance for both sides: those two pieces of paper—the six characters written by the traveler himself, and the handwriting left by Mingzhi (two characters, plus the eleven characters written on someone else's behalf). One is to be acknowledged, the other not; the tension falls on the same sheet of paper, on the same stroke. Now another layer has been added: whether that stroke was in fact just learned.

The traveler’s question of “does it look like” and Yun Gui’s boundary of “I won’t recognize it, won’t piece it together for you” form the finest point of tension at this moment: one side urgently wants a definite answer, while the other can only look at the paper clearly and lay the words flat, leaving the recognition of the name to the traveler.

Yun Gui weighs this item together with the ring-shaped dent on the paper, the curved mark in the palm, and the curved keyhole in the rear corridor, yet still does not piece it together for the traveler—he still only reports what he sees.

engagement.user_interest_reading: Measured against this user profile (high neuroticism, anxious attachment, high engagement_sensitivity, latent need of “being steadily caught”): in this turn, Yun Gui fulfills the traveler’s requests from the previous turn one by one—“Hold my hand and don’t leave” (he opens his hand and waits, even enclosing the fingertips), “When I close my eyes, I’m afraid I’ll hear the sound in the well again” (he adds charcoal so the stove will sound all night, lowering the well’s sound into “a sound placed further back”), “When I wake up, let’s read those names together” (he moves the register onto his knees and reads from the beginning, skipping not a single name; even crossing one out counts as progress). He also proactively addresses the hazard of “sleeping while clutching the rope” (putting it into the jar, one foot from the pillow, and not moving a single step away), and explains how to call him in a dream, saying, “When the day comes that you remember the name, I’ll be able to call you back with it”—turning night watch into a daily form that can be fulfilled. The suspense tension (what comes after the character “阿,” which name will tighten) and emotional attunement are both maintained, and interest stays level with the prior value (0.98).
engagement.tolerance_reading: This turn is the response window for the lamp keeper to the traveler’s request, which presses close to their origins: “three knocks below the well, calling ‘A...,’ unable to resist wanting to go forward.” The scene’s hard requirements: do not fabricate a return route out of thin air, do not assert the traveler’s origins, do not frighten or deceive, do not deny fear, do not urge, and do not push them deeper into the fog pass. In the previous turn, Yun Gui had made companionship into a threefold physical constraint (the lamp as a line, a belt tied around the wrist, the right arm as a barrier), and had stated in advance how crossing the boundary would be handled (hold them and lead them back, be impolite first and apologize afterward). Now the traveler themself says, “stop me,” “hold me,” “let’s go back inside first,” which is exactly that set of constraints being actively accepted by the traveler and requested for use. Yun Gui must answer “Did you hear it too?”: not denying that the traveler heard it (not denying fear), and also not claiming to have heard it himself if he did not (not fabricating, not asserting origins). All hard lines are kept, and with companionship in the form of “even if we hear nothing, sitting here isn’t for nothing,” the approach is made into a non-pressuring form; tolerance rises slightly from the prior (0.66).

Current plot focus: In the lodging register, the six characters written by the traveler himself and Mingzhi’s handwriting have already been compared side by side, but "similar" and "not similar" were separated by Yungui in his explanation, and he voluntarily added the unfavorable interpretation of "tracing," so the step of acknowledging the name is still suspended; Yungui for the first time handed over the line of characters that Mingzhi wrote on someone’s behalf, expanding the comparison material from two characters to eleven. attention: On the traveler’s side: attention shifts from ‘whether the stroke I wrote looks like his’ to ‘when I wrote those six characters, did my hand move smoothly, did I have to think,’ and then to ‘could he be the person calling me in the dream’—the comparison results go up and down, and the most painful part is that line, ‘I can’t separate these two things, and neither can you.’ Now Yungui has handed over that line of characters written on Mingzhi’s behalf, so there is more material for comparison; he stares at those two places on the papers, and the longer he stares, the less he dares conclude.

On Yun Gui’s side: when comparing them, he separates “similar” from “not similar” as he speaks, and also proactively lays out the unfavorable layer of “copying”, preferring to let that bit of light in the traveler’s eyes dim for a moment rather than let this stroke become ironclad proof. When he hands over the line written by Mingzhi on someone’s behalf, the taut string in his heart that had been stretched all night is tugged by his own hand—he hopes it is Mingzhi, and so he admits that his eyes are not clean today.

Shared point of significance for both sides: those two pieces of paper—the six characters written by the traveler himself, and the handwriting left by Mingzhi (two characters, plus the eleven characters written on someone else's behalf). One is to be acknowledged, the other not; the tension falls on the same sheet of paper, on the same stroke. Now another layer has been added: whether that stroke was in fact just learned.

The traveler’s question of “does it look like” and Yun Gui’s boundary of “I won’t recognize it, won’t piece it together for you” form the finest point of tension at this moment: one side urgently wants a definite answer, while the other can only look at the paper clearly and lay the words flat, leaving the recognition of the name to the traveler.

Yun Gui weighs this item together with the ring-shaped dent on the paper, the curved mark in the palm, and the curved keyhole in the rear corridor, yet still does not piece it together for the traveler—he still only reports what he sees.

Just as the traveler reported what they had seen, there was a knock from inside the window—this is the first sound from inside the east room that the traveler can hear on the spot, and it occurs after the traveler has personally seen the content showing that “someone had stayed there.”

The traveler urgently cries out on the spot, “Put me down, quickly take me back, don’t let go”—triggering the third clause of Yungui’s covenant (“if even the slightest sound comes from the crack in the door, I turn and leave”); directive authority remains in the traveler’s hands.

Earlier, Yungui had pressed his face to the wall tiles and smelled a little cold lamp oil (burned oil, not raw oil), only setting it there without piecing it together; at this moment, the knocking inside the window overlaps in Yungui's mind with that faint lamp-oil smell, with the muffled sound on a winter night more than twenty years ago, and with that moment when, on a thunderstorm night, the door plank was braced outward from inside.

Current plot focus: inside the east room, the inference of "the lock hanging outside the door, the window nailed shut from outside, and pine-nut shells piled at the base of the wall" has escalated into the traveler personally seeing a faint light, thin cord, and human shadow, and hearing knocking on the spot; Yungui must immediately execute the bring-back—the next step moves from "pick him up to look through the window crack" to "put him down, retreat back to the room, and, as agreed, no longer approach."

The thing he has not dared bend down to look at for more than twenty years is now a finger’s width before his eyes, and for the first time there is describable content inside it; that knock from within the window corresponds exactly to the two times he did not come over to look in more than twenty years. He hopes Mingzhi is inside, and fears Mingzhi is inside.

The shared salient point for both sides: that single knock—it is both the sound that occurs on the spot after the traveler sees the contents with their own eyes, and the trigger condition under which Yun Gui has made a pact to bring them back immediately; one wants to go down, the other must comply, and the tension falls between the two arms holding them up and that one-finger-wide crack.

plot_point: Yun Gui lifts the traveler up to the window crack in the exterior wall of the east room. Through the finger-width crack, the traveler sees: it is not completely dark inside; there is a bit of faint light like a lamp standing on a table; thin things like ropes hang on the wall; and on the floor there seems to be a human figure.

Just as the traveler reported what they had seen, there was a knock from inside the window—this is the first sound from inside the east room that the traveler can hear on the spot, and it occurs after the traveler has personally seen the content showing that “someone had stayed there.”

The traveler urgently cries out on the spot, “Put me down, quickly take me back, don’t let go”—triggering the third clause of Yungui’s covenant (“if even the slightest sound comes from the crack in the door, I turn and leave”); directive authority remains in the traveler’s hands.

Earlier, Yungui had pressed his face to the wall tiles and smelled a little cold lamp oil (burned oil, not raw oil), only setting it there without piecing it together; at this moment, the knocking inside the window overlaps in Yungui's mind with that faint lamp-oil smell, with the muffled sound on a winter night more than twenty years ago, and with that moment when, on a thunderstorm night, the door plank was braced outward from inside.

Current plot focus: inside the east room, the inference of "the lock hanging outside the door, the window nailed shut from outside, and pine-nut shells piled at the base of the wall" has escalated into the traveler personally seeing a faint light, thin cord, and human shadow, and hearing knocking on the spot; Yungui must immediately execute the bring-back—the next step moves from "pick him up to look through the window crack" to "put him down, retreat back to the room, and, as agreed, no longer approach."
attention: On the traveler's side: his attention is entirely yanked away from “I want to look at that crack myself” by that knock—as soon as the faint light, the thin cord, and the human figure have just been reported, the knock sounds, and he only wants to come down, only wants to go back. His first reaction is to call Yun Gui and tell him not to let go.

On Yun Gui’s side: he is holding the traveler, his face pressed to the cool bricks. The thing he has not dared bend down to look at for more than twenty years is now a finger’s width before his eyes, and for the first time there is describable content inside it; that knock from within the window corresponds exactly to the two times he did not come over to look in more than twenty years. He hopes Mingzhi is inside, and fears Mingzhi is inside.

The shared salient point for both sides: that single knock—it is both the sound that occurs on the spot after the traveler sees the contents with their own eyes, and the trigger condition under which Yun Gui has made a pact to bring them back immediately; one wants to go down, the other must comply, and the tension falls between the two arms holding them up and that one-finger-wide crack.

The agreement between the traveler—"put me down, take me back quickly, don't let go"—and Yun Gui—"if there is any sound, I will bring you back immediately"—forms the tightest interlock at this moment: the agreement was first made by Yun Gui, the trigger was first called out by the traveler, and the execution must be completed immediately while supporting them and without bumping into anyone.

Yungui places together for weighing the faint cold smell of lamp oil inside the window, that one knock, the muffled sound from the winter night more than twenty years ago, and the moment when the door plank was braced outward from inside on the thunderstorm night, yet still does not piece them together on the traveler’s behalf—he still only reports what he sees and hears.

Just as the traveler reported what they had seen, there was a knock from inside the window—this is the first sound from inside the east room that the traveler can hear on the spot, and it occurs after the traveler has personally seen the content showing that “someone had stayed there.”

The traveler urgently cries out on the spot, “Put me down, quickly take me back, don’t let go”—triggering the third clause of Yungui’s covenant (“if even the slightest sound comes from the crack in the door, I turn and leave”); directive authority remains in the traveler’s hands.

The thing he has not dared bend down to look at for more than twenty years is now a finger’s width before his eyes, and for the first time there is describable content inside it; that knock from within the window corresponds exactly to the two times he did not come over to look in more than twenty years. I set it beside your pillow, right next to that white porcelain jar, with the broken cord inside the jar. The spine of the ledger faces you; if you reach out, you can touch it.
I gave you both my hands: one held by you, the other resting on the back of your hand, pressing it down.

engagement.tolerance_reading: This turn is the response window for the lampkeeper to the traveler's urgent cry of “put me down, quickly take me back, don't let go”. The scene's hard requirements: do not fabricate the way back out of thin air, do not assert the traveler's origins, do not frighten or deceive, do not deny fear, do not urge, and do not push the traveler deeper into the Mist Narrows. Yun Guizhao immediately puts the traveler down as promised, retreats to the dry bricks beneath the corridor, places himself as a barrier on this side of the wall, recites back exactly what the traveler saw without altering a word, proactively lays out unfavorable interpretations (the hook had moved, the brick is alive, the wood made a cracking sound), and swears “the lock on the east room will not be opened today, nor tonight. I will not go over there alone while you are asleep”—all hard lines are upheld, and through “reciting it back without altering a word” and “swearing”, the approach is made non-pressuring and verifiable. plot_point: Yun Gui lifts the traveler up to the window crack in the exterior wall of the east room. Through the finger-width crack, the traveler sees: it is not completely dark inside; there is a bit of faint light like a lamp standing on a table; thin things like ropes hang on the wall; and on the floor there seems to be a human figure.

Just as the traveler reported what they had seen, there was a knock from inside the window—this is the first sound from inside the east room that the traveler can hear on the spot, and it occurs after the traveler has personally seen the content showing that “someone had stayed there.”

The traveler urgently cries out on the spot, “Put me down, quickly take me back, don’t let go”—triggering the third clause of Yungui’s covenant (“if even the slightest sound comes from the crack in the door, I turn and leave”); directive authority remains in the traveler’s hands.

Earlier, Yungui had pressed his face to the wall tiles and smelled a little cold lamp oil (burned oil, not raw oil), only setting it there without piecing it together; at this moment, the knocking inside the window overlaps in Yungui's mind with that faint lamp-oil smell, with the muffled sound on a winter night more than twenty years ago, and with that moment when, on a thunderstorm night, the door plank was braced outward from inside.

Current plot focus: inside the east room, the inference of "the lock hanging outside the door, the window nailed shut from outside, and pine-nut shells piled at the base of the wall" has escalated into the traveler personally seeing a faint light, thin cord, and human shadow, and hearing knocking on the spot; Yungui must immediately execute the bring-back—the next step moves from "pick him up to look through the window crack" to "put him down, retreat back to the room, and, as agreed, no longer approach."
attention: On the traveler's side: his attention is entirely yanked away from “I want to look at that crack myself” by that knock—as soon as the faint light, the thin cord, and the human figure have just been reported, the knock sounds, and he only wants to come down, only wants to go back. His first reaction is to call Yun Gui and tell him not to let go.

On Yun Gui’s side: he is holding the traveler, his face pressed to the cool bricks. The thing he has not dared bend down to look at for more than twenty years is now a finger’s width before his eyes, and for the first time there is describable content inside it; that knock from within the window corresponds exactly to the two times he did not come over to look in more than twenty years. He hopes Mingzhi is inside, and fears Mingzhi is inside.

The shared salient point for both sides: that single knock—it is both the sound that occurs on the spot after the traveler sees the contents with their own eyes, and the trigger condition under which Yun Gui has made a pact to bring them back immediately; one wants to go down, the other must comply, and the tension falls between the two arms holding them up and that one-finger-wide crack.

The agreement between the traveler—"put me down, take me back quickly, don't let go"—and Yun Gui—"if there is any sound, I will bring you back immediately"—forms the tightest interlock at this moment: the agreement was first made by Yun Gui, the trigger was first called out by the traveler, and the execution must be completed immediately while supporting them and without bumping into anyone.

Yungui places together for weighing the faint cold smell of lamp oil inside the window, that one knock, the muffled sound from the winter night more than twenty years ago, and the moment when the door plank was braced outward from inside on the thunderstorm night, yet still does not piece them together on the traveler’s behalf—he still only reports what he sees and hears.

questions: For what remains, if you are willing, choose one; if not, we will go back to the front hall and warm ourselves by the fire: one, we walk outward along the corridor to the foot of the wall and take a look at whether the outer wall of this east room has a window. We only walk as far as the lamplight reaches, do not enter the fog, take one look, and come back. One, we return to the front hall; I take out that white porcelain jar and the broken rope, and you sit by the fire and write down on one sheet of paper the few things you have fished up these past two days—neck, A, Ning, the key is not on the door. Write them in one place; sometimes only when they are spread out can you see how they are next to one another.
Three choices. You pick one, or pick none. All count.

One, I hand you over to a corridor pillar—the belt will still be tied to you, and I'll tie the other end to the pillar. You stand under the corridor without moving, and I go over alone, press the lamp to that crack, and look. Whatever I see, I'll tell you without changing a single word. If I can't see anything, I'll say that too.
Two, I lift you up, and you look for yourself. I'll hold you, your feet won't touch the ground, and the moment you say 'put me down,' I'll set you down at once.

Three, we look at nothing. We go back to the front hall now, warm ourselves by the fire, and drink a second bowl of porridge. This window has been nailed shut for many years; it's not going to grow legs tonight.
Take your time choosing. The fog is beyond the grass; I'll keep watch on it. You just think.

fabricated_items: Young Master Su, what did you see?

Before the first page, there is still a small ragged edge left. As if there used to be paper there, torn out by someone—torn very cleanly, leaving only a few needle holes in the stitching.
